title: async/await Fundamentals
summary: Compose asynchronous operations without blocking request threads, and distinguish await from background-thread execution.
objectives: Explain what await does to the flow of an asynchronous method.
Distinguish asynchronous I/O from work running on a background thread.
Explain why .Result and .Wait() are the wrong default in request code.

sections.heading: Async is not a background thread
Why .Result and .Wait() are not the default

reviewCandidates.prompt: What happens to an ASP.NET Core request thread while a handler awaits a database call?
reviewCandidates.answer: The thread is released back to the thread pool and can serve other requests while the I/O is in flight. When the operation completes, the method resumes, possibly on a different thread.

reviewCandidates.prompt: Does awaiting an asynchronous database call run the work on a background thread?
reviewCandidates.answer: No. Asynchronous I/O releases the waiting thread instead of starting a new one. Async is about not holding threads during waits, not about running work in parallel.

reviewCandidates.prompt: Why are .Result and .Wait() usually the wrong default in ASP.NET Core request code?
reviewCandidates.answer: They block a thread pool thread for the entire wait. Under load, blocked threads accumulate and can starve the thread pool, increasing latency for all requests. await pauses the method without holding a thread.
